name: AnimatedGIF
language: C (C99 core with an Arduino-style C++ class wrapper)
workload: Decode time of an 8-frame 160x120 GIF (badgers.h) on microcontroller boards in perf.png; the 2-30x figure compares the library's own Turbo mode with its own Normal mode.
claimed_speedup: README: new Turbo decode mode (output image used as the LZW dictionary, needs another 32K of RAM) 'can accelerate the decoding by 2-30x depending on the target system and image' (versus the library's own Normal mode, not versus libgif). Against libgif the README says only that the code 'will perform far better than libgif', with no number.
hardware: perf.png lists MCU boards only: ESP8266 80 MHz 158,961 us; ESP32-S2 240 MHz 58,902 us; ESP32 240 MHz 49,468 us; Cortex-M0+ 48 MHz 357,160 us; Cortex-M4F 64 MHz 181,122 us; Cortex-M7 600 MHz 8,134 us. No desktop CPU stated.
tradeoffs: Turbo mode trades about 32K of extra RAM for speed; core needs only 24K RAM in normal mode, no malloc/free, line-by-line callback API built for SPI LCDs. Some GIFs (alternating transparent and opaque pixels, local palettes in COOKED mode) need a full canvas or run slower in the low-RAM modes. README says it does not use CPU-specific optimizations or assembly.
caveats: No numeric comparison against any recognizable baseline was found: perf.png is a table that compares boards with each other (a speed rating relative to Cortex-M0+), no libgif or giflib column. The 2-30x claim is Turbo versus the library's own Normal mode, with no table, harness, compiler, flags or image set behind it. README says the library performs far better than libgif on PC-class devices but gives no figure; the wiki (single Home page, 'Normal vs Turbo Mode') has no numbers either, and the linux/ directory holds only a Makefile and examples. Author's blog post 'A Big Memory GIF Decoder' is blocked here. Same Turbo LZW technique as the already-listed giflib-turbo (same author), which carries the drop-in giflib comparison. Tier D kept for the record; the project is notable (537 stars).

name: qoi-asm
language: x86-64 assembly (GNU as, Intel syntax) with a C test and benchmark harness
baseline: QOI reference implementation qoi.h (phoboslab/qoi) compiled with gcc -O3 -march=x86-64-v3
workload: Encode and decode of 7 generated inputs (1080p and 512x512, RGB and RGBA: random, runs, photo-like gradient plus noise, 16-colour palette), 18 rows, median of 11 reps (images of 1 Mpx or more) or 31 reps, timed with lfence/rdtsc and clock_gettime.
claimed_speedup: 1.07x-2.16x faster than gcc -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 on all 18 benchmark rows (examples: 1080p RGBA random encode 1.95x, 1080p RGBA photo-like encode 1.83x, 512x512 RGBA random decode to 4 channels 2.16x, 512x512 RGB photo-like decode to 3 channels 1.07x); also 1.57x-3.47x over its own first assembly port.
compiler_and_flags: Baseline C is the untouched c/qoi.c built with gcc -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 (gcc version not stated); an -O2 build is also timed; harness built with gcc -O2 -g -Wall -Wextra; assembly assembled with GNU as. Reproduce with make bench BENCH_CMD='taskset -c 3 ./build/bench'.
hardware: Intel Core i7-14700F (Raptor Lake, AVX2, no AVX-512), WSL2 Linux kernel 5.15, pinned with taskset -c 3; invariant TSC about 2.07-2.08 GHz.
tradeoffs: Requires x86-64-v3 (Haswell 2013 or newer): older CPUs raise SIGILL, no ARM or other ISA, GNU as only. Drop-in for the four qoi.h symbols (qoi_encode, qoi_decode, qoi_write, qoi_read) with no algorithmic change, so the format and compression ratio are the same as qoi.h. Like qoi.h, qoi_decode may read a few bytes past the end on a truncated stream.
caveats: Outputs are bit-identical to qoi.h: bench.c compares ref, -O3 and asm output bit for bit before timing (bench_after_D1.txt prints 'all encode/decode outputs bit-identical') and the repo reports 19,185 differential cases plus ASan and UBSan runs. Weaknesses: single host under WSL2; inputs are generated (the 'photo-like' images are synthetic gradients plus noise, not real photographs); cycles are invariant-TSC ticks that can understate core cycles by up to 2.4x, so only ratios and ns/op mean anything (run-to-run drift 6-8 percent); the baseline is qoi.h, not libpng, libwebp or the other listed incumbents, and no real-image corpus (qoibench) was used. README says it was produced by a multi-agent LLM workflow; the 'independent verifier' mentioned is part of that workflow. One commit, zero stars, published 2026-09-26, no outside reproduction.

name: rusty_jpeg
baseline: FFmpeg 8.1.2 native MJPEG encoder and decoder (not libjpeg-turbo)
workload: Encode: 40-frame 1920x1080 4:2:0 clip at about 680 KB per frame to MJPEG at matched output size with fixed Huffman tables on both sides. Decode: one photographic still stream-copied to 300 frames, both arms discarding output. One pinned core each, CPU time, paired interleaved runs.
claimed_speedup: No speedup: README states parity with FFmpeg. Encode median 0.96x (N=41, z -3.59, ours output 3.1% smaller); decode median 1.02x (N=31, z -0.18, inside noise). WHYS.md gives the ratio as FFmpeg time over ours, so encode is about 4% slower and decode about 2% faster. CHANGES.md says earlier claims of 1.19x-1.45x faster were small-N artifacts and were withdrawn.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Cargo.toml has no custom release profile; default features enable AVX2/SSE4.1 kernels with runtime detection (NEON on aarch64). FFmpeg run with -threads 1 per WHYS.md.
hardware: CPU model not stated; one pinned core; the author notes the test box drifts about 15 percent. Harness scripts in WHYS.md are PowerShell (.ps1).
stars_or_usage: 1 star; README claims 2,784 active installs (RAG Converter runs it as WebAssembly)
tradeoffs: no_std plus alloc builds for ESP32-class chips; x86 AVX2 DCT and SSSE3 IDCT kernels are not bit-identical to the scalar twins (plus or minus 1 LSB); trellis quantization is off by default because it costs +144% encode time; optimized Huffman tables give -7.4% size for 2.09x encode time; chroma is box-averaged on downsample, so output differs from FFmpeg's. IJG attribution clause applies to the forward-DCT files.
caveats: Not faster than the baseline: the project's own final standing is parity, and its encode test (N=41) reads about 4% slower. Checks asked for in the lead: threads, one pinned core and ffmpeg -threads 1, but WHYS.md records that the 'single-threaded' ours arm was silently multithreaded until it was repaired (and an earlier 'decode faster' reading came from extra cores); timer is pinned CPU time; decode input bitstream and per-frame checksums are identical across arms per WHYS.md, while encode outputs differ (matched size only, no output hash comparison). Reproducibility is poor: the paired.ps1 and paired2.ps1 harness scripts are not in the repo tree (examples/ holds decode_bench.rs and others), the CPU and rustc settings are missing, and FFmpeg is a different baseline from libjpeg-turbo. WHYS.md also documents several void measurements and a trellis cost claim off by 46x. The crate is a vendored merge of jpeg-decoder 0.3.2 and jpeg-encoder 0.7.0 (vstroebel) with its own AVX2 and fused decode-IDCT changes; not a GitHub fork. Kept as a flagged entry.

name: rusty_gif
baseline: FFmpeg 8.1.2 GIF encode via palettegen/paletteuse (dither=none, high-quality path) and FFmpeg's GIF decoder
workload: Encode of 8 real-content frames (CIF to 1080p) with content-routed quantization versus FFmpeg's palettegen/paletteuse; pinned CPU time, interleaved A/B, 15 rounds; PSNR scored against the FFmpeg result. Decode workload not described.
claimed_speedup: README: 1.5-2.5x faster encode at higher PSNR on 8/8 benchmark frames (0.40-0.67x of FFmpeg's CPU time, PSNR +0.2 to +4.1 dB, 15/15 paired wins per frame); decode 'up to 2.5x faster' with no table or workload.
tradeoffs: #![forbid(unsafe_code)] throughout; LZW is the external pure-Rust weezl crate. The quantizer is output-changing (exact palette up to 256 colours, k-means up to 65,536, budget NeuQuant above) so palettes differ from upstream gif and from FFmpeg; RUSTY_GIF_Q_POLICY=upstream reproduces the pre-fork output byte for byte.
caveats: The speedup comes from a cheaper quantizer, not a faster LZW coder, and the quality side is judged by PSNR, which the k-means step is built to minimize. Not reproducible from the repo: the pinned ABBA harness is referenced in UPSTREAM-CHANGES.md ('see repo bench notes') but is not in this repo, whose examples/ holds only encode_bench.rs (times rusty_gif alone, single frame, and depends on the rusty_alloc-api 1.1.6 dev-dependency) and stage_profile.rs; CPU, compiler flags, FFmpeg build and thread settings are not given; decode claim has no numbers; no comparison against giflib or the listed baselines. Performance fork of image-rs/image-gif (gif 0.14.2 plus color_quant 1.1.0), which has no benchmark data in its page. Kept as a first-party claim, tier C.

name: bcdec
baseline: DirectXTex BCn decoders (also Compressonator and bc7enc_rdo decoders)
workload: BC1, BC3, BC6H and BC7 block decompression speed in Mpix/s; the only numbers opened are before/after figures for bcdec's own optimization, not a cross-library table.
claimed_speedup: No opened number against a named external decoder. PR #1 by aras-p (merged 2022-06-23), bcdec before to after: Windows VS2022 on Ryzen 5950X BC1 821 to 1327 Mpix/s, BC3 516 to 694, BC6H 65 to 85, BC7 91 to 143; macOS Clang 13 on M1 Max BC1 804 to 2037, BC3 585 to 1062, BC6H 63 to 76, BC7 113 to 212. README credits that work with up to 3x speed on BC1/BC3.
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2022 on Windows and Clang 13 on macOS per PR #1; flags not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5950X and Apple M1 Max per PR #1.
tradeoffs: Single-header C, no allocation, no external dependencies, minimal stack; BC1-BC7 including BC6H (float or half output). README says it was 'never optimized specifically for speed but for the overall size'. Dual licensed MIT or Unlicense.
caveats: No cross-library figure could be opened. aras-p's independent 'Comparing BCn texture decoders' (2022-06-23, code at https://github.com/aras-p/bcn_decoder_tester with amd_cmp, bc7enc_rdo, bcdec, convection, DirectXTex, icbc, etcpak, mesa, squish, swiftshader; measured on Apple M1 Max) is blocked here (EGRESS_BLOCKED on aras-p.info) and the repo carries no results table; a search snippet says bcdec is the easiest to use and fast in most cases but that bc7enc_rdo's decoder is fastest for BC7 and etcpak for BC1/BC3, so bcdec is not the fastest across the board. Needs a re-check from an environment that reaches that blog: the table may support a tier A or B ratio against DirectXTex and Compressonator. The project itself disclaims speed as a goal. Tier D here; kept because the seed list asked for it.
